title: Four kinds of happiness
hookLine: having wealth, using it well, owing no debt, and being blameless (AN 4.62)
last: FIVE TRADES — WHAT YOUR MONEY DOES.

cards: A merchant covers a whole park in gold coins, by the old story, to buy it for the Buddha's community.

His name is Anathapindika, of the city of Savatthi, and it means feeder of the unprotected, for all the food he gave away. So when the Buddha talks to him about money, he isn't lecturing someone on thrift.
He's talking to a man with more than enough. And he names four kinds of happiness that wealth can touch, and says one of them outweighs the other three put together.

teach.b: The first is the happiness of having: wealth earned, the sutta says, by hard work, by the strength of your arms and the sweat of your brow, rightly gained. It counts as a real happiness.
The Buddha doesn't tell a householder that money is shameful.
The second is the happiness of using it: enjoying your wealth and doing good with it, for yourself, your family, your friends and worthy causes. Money sitting untouched is only half a pleasure.
The third is owing nothing, no debt, large or small. A credit card bill that keeps growing shows what it's like when this one is missing.
The fourth is blamelessness: knowing that what you've done with body, speech and mind carries no fault. Then the closing verse.
The first three, the Buddha says, aren't worth a sixteenth part of the fourth, an old Indian idiom for a tiny fraction. It isn't a choice between them; a householder can have all four.
The sutta simply ranks them. You can be wealthy, generous and debt-free, and still uneasy if you know how the money was made.
And you can have very little, owe nothing, and sleep like a stone, because there's nothing in your day you need to hide.

how: Buddhist teachers use this sutta to show that householders may rightly enjoy honestly earned wealth, while counting a clear conscience as the greatest happiness; Anathapindika is remembered in the tradition as the model generous lay follower.

o: the happiness of a life with nothing to hide
the happiness of being free from all debt
the joy of giving your wealth to the needy

games.q: the four kinds of happiness: tap the pairs.
p: what the first three are worth

s: the Buddha told Anathapindika that wealth is shameful
he calls having wealth rightly gained a real happiness.
owing no debt is one of the four kinds of happiness
the happiness of freedom from debt is the third.
the four are a choice: you can only have one
a householder can have all four; the sutta ranks them, with blamelessness first.

games.q: you're Anathapindika, a wealthy merchant of Savatthi. of the four kinds of happiness, which does the Buddha say is worth the most?
games.why: in AN 4.62 the Buddha says the first three aren't worth a sixteenth part of the happiness of blamelessness.

practice: Go through the four slowly and look for a trace of each in your own life: something you have, however small; something you used well or shared; a debt paid off, or never taken on; something you did this week that you don't need to hide.
Rest longest on whichever one you find, and let it be a real happiness, the way the sutta says it is.

wordCard.voice: Anavajja-sukha, the happiness of blamelessness. Having, using, owing nothing, and blamelessness; the Buddha tells Anathapindika the last outweighs the rest.

orig.note: Pali anavajja-sukha: the happiness of blamelessness, the fourth and greatest in AN 4.62.

carryVoice: Your line: blameless is best. Wealth is a real happiness, and a clear conscience is a bigger one. Day three hundred seventy-nine, done.

sources.ref: Vinaya, Cullavagga VI (Anathapindika buys Jeta's Grove)
